reference.title: Lying Around the World
reference.listing: Page could not be read here (gymvisual.com is blocked by the proxy); the movement is taken from the exercise name and standard coaching practice.

breathing.pattern: Breathe steadily; exhale as the legs pass the low side of the circle.
breathing.cadence: One breath per circle, about 3 s

prescription.progression: Bigger circles, lower bottom point, slower circles

cues.text: Lie on your back, arms by your sides, palms down. Lift both straight legs together.
Draw a big circle with the feet: up, out to one side, down, across, and back up.
Keep the legs glued together and the pelvis and shoulders still on the mat.
Lower the legs together with control.

mistakes.fix: Make the circle smaller; press the palms and the back of the shoulders into the mat.

mistakes.mistake: Low back arching at the bottom of the circle
mistakes.fix: Keep the bottom of the circle higher.
Squeeze the knees and ankles together.
Slow, even circles, about 3 s each.

kinematics.norm: Circle centred well off the floor; the bottom stays high enough for a flat low back (clinical opinion)
Legs swing about 20-25 degrees to each side with the pelvis still (clinical opinion)

sources.title: GymVisual #9012, Lying Around the World, video (movement reference; page not readable here)
Andersson, Nilsson, Ma and Thorstensson 1997, abdominal and hip flexor muscle activation during various training exercises (Eur J Appl Physiol 75:115-123; PMID 9118976)
Drysdale, Earl and Hertel 2004, surface EMG of the abdominal muscles during pelvic-tilt and abdominal-hollowing exercises (J Athl Train 39(1):32-36)
Escamilla et al. 2016, muscle activation among supine, prone and side position exercises with and without a Swiss ball (Sports Health 8(4):372-379)

cautions: Stop if you feel sharp, radiating or nerve-type pain.
Muscle glow colours and activation curves are illustrative, not measured EMG.
If the low back arches off the mat, the legs are too low for your strength: raise them or bend the knees.
modify: Hands under the buttocks help keep the pelvis tilted and the low back down.
Bend the knees a little to shorten the lever.
Pregnancy, postpartum or diastasis recti: get cleared first, and avoid long supine work later in pregnancy.
regressions: One leg at a time, the other foot flat.
progressions: Bigger circles with a lower bottom point.
Arms overhead instead of by the sides.

muscleNotes.core: Rectus abdominis and transversus abdominis keep the pelvis from tipping forward and the low back from arching while the legs move (Drysdale 2004: highest abdominal activity in pelvic-tilt work with the legs unsupported).
muscleNotes.hip_flexors_r: Iliopsoas and rectus femoris hold the legs up against gravity (clinical opinion; hip flexor EMG rises with leg-lowering work, Andersson 1997).
muscleNotes.hip_flexors_l: Iliopsoas and rectus femoris hold the legs up against gravity (clinical opinion; hip flexor EMG rises with leg-lowering work, Andersson 1997).
muscleNotes.obliques_r: As the legs swing to one side, the obliques stop the pelvis rolling after them (clinical opinion).
muscleNotes.obliques_l: As the legs swing to one side, the obliques stop the pelvis rolling after them (clinical opinion).
muscleNotes.adductors_r: Squeeze the legs together so they move as one (clinical opinion).
muscleNotes.adductors_l: Squeeze the legs together so they move as one (clinical opinion).
muscleNotes.quads_r: Keep the knees straight and the legs long (clinical opinion).
muscleNotes.quads_l: Keep the knees straight and the legs long (clinical opinion).
